html:
A Doric temple on a hilltop on the island of Aegina, built around 500 BCE for Aphaia, a local goddess. Many of its columns still stand.

Its two pediments showed battles of the Trojan War, with Athena in the middle. They are famous because they show Greek sculpture changing. The figures on the west end keep the stiff archaic smile even when dying. The east end, carved a little later, has a dying warrior whose body and face show real pain, an early sign of the Classical style seen later at the Temple of Zeus at Olympia and the Parthenon.

The temple was built when Aegina was a rich trading power with its own coins, before Athens defeated it. The sculptures were dug up in 1811 and bought by Crown Prince Ludwig of Bavaria. They are now in the Glyptothek in Munich.
sum: A Doric temple on a hilltop on the island of Aegina, built around 500 BCE for Aphaia, a local goddess. Many of its columns still stand.
